required: Recommends one procedure from the sensible ones: Token Ring, p-persistent CSMA, non-persistent CSMA, CSMA/CD or TDMA with reservation (any one of these is enough).

First reason: a property of the chosen procedure that fits this scenario (high channel load, tight budget, 20 systems, expandable), stated with what makes it an advantage, e.g. scalability, extendability, cost, throughput under load, low hardware needs. A bare property name without its link to the scenario does not count.
Second reason: a different advantage, also tied to the scenario and to the chosen procedure.
One weakness of the chosen procedure that is really true of it (e.g. waiting time, overhead, complexity, hardware needs, constraints), with what makes it a weakness.
wrong: Recommending a procedure outside the sensible ones (e.g. Pure or Slotted ALOHA, 1-persistent CSMA, Polling).
A reason or weakness that does not hold for the procedure chosen.
not_required: Which of the sensible procedures is picked, and which particular properties from the lecture's list are used.
Numbers about the 20 systems.

required: Yes: this routing strategy can cause a problem at the receiver.

Why: with load as the metric the best path keeps changing as traffic moves onto it, so routes fluctuate or oscillate between the alternative paths when there is more than one path between two end systems (here via CF and EI).
The effect at the receiver: packets of one transfer take different paths and arrive out of order (packet reordering).
wrong: Saying there is no problem, or that the load metric gives stable routes.
Saying reordering happens without tying it to routes changing between several paths.
not_required: Naming the exact links CF and EI.
Other drawbacks of load-based routing.

required: Connectionless is the better choice.
Why: the user talks to many different partners (websites), each only for a short time.
A connection set up and torn down for every website skimmed would cost a lot of overhead for very short data transfers.
wrong: Choosing connection-oriented.
Choosing connectionless with a reason that contradicts the notes, e.g. that connections are never needed on the web.
not_required: Details of the connect and disconnect phases.
Mentioning specific protocols.

required: Flow pipeline (flow tables): holds rules (match fields and the actions to take) that decide how packets are forwarded, i.e. it implements the routing logic in the switch.
Meter table: holds a meter entry per flow / collects flow statistics, which the controller uses to manage the network, e.g. QoS such as rate limiting.
wrong: Swapping the two roles (meter table forwarding packets, flow tables measuring).
Anything that contradicts the notes.
not_required: Rate limiting specifically, the word QoS, or the exact number of tables.

required: Names the two phases: slow start and congestion avoidance.
Slow start (cwnd below ss_thresh): cwnd grows by one for every acknowledged segment, which is exponential growth (cwnd doubles each round trip).
Congestion avoidance (cwnd at or above ss_thresh): cwnd grows more slowly, roughly linearly (e.g. one more after all sent segments are acknowledged).
The switch: slow start lasts until ss_thresh is reached (or a loss); from then on it is congestion avoidance.
On packet loss or congestion, in either phase: ss_thresh is set to cwnd / 2 and cwnd is reset to 1 (so slow start starts again).
wrong: Slow start growing linearly or congestion avoidance growing exponentially.
ss_thresh set to cwnd, or left unchanged, after a loss.
cwnd not being reset to 1 after a loss.
not_required: Other increment strategies for congestion avoidance.
The exact initial values.

required: Names the two phases: slow start and congestion avoidance.
Slow start: ss_thresh stays constant while cwnd is increased by one for every acknowledged segment until ss_thresh is reached.
After ss_thresh is reached the increase of cwnd becomes slower (congestion avoidance).
On loss or congestion: ss_thresh is set to cwnd / 2 first, and then cwnd is reset to 1.
wrong: ss_thresh changing during slow start growth.
ss_thresh set to cwnd, or not adjusted, when cwnd is reset to 1.
Anything that contradicts the notes.
not_required: Exponential versus linear terminology, round trip details.

required: The order from least to most probable is B, C, A.

A justification that holds, one of: B is a special case (subset) of C and C a special case of A, i.e. each is more specific than the next; or a correct calculation or formula showing P(B) < P(C) < P(A) (e.g. P(B) = 0.6^3 * 0.4^3 = 0.0138, P(C) = 20 * P(B), P(A) = P(C) + P(4 H) + P(5 H) + P(6 H)).
wrong: Any other order.
A justification that is wrong, e.g. that the events are equally likely or that the more specific event is more probable.
not_required: The full numeric calculation if the ordering is clearly justified, and rounding beyond two decimals.

required: Names the three classes: unconfirmed connectionless, confirmed connectionless, connection-oriented.
Unconfirmed connectionless: no acknowledgement, so data can be lost; no flow control; no connect or disconnect.
Confirmed connectionless: acknowledgements, and a timeout and retransmit, so no data is lost; no flow control; no connect or disconnect.
Because confirmed connectionless retransmits, duplicates and sequence errors are still possible.
Connection-oriented: no loss, duplicates or sequence errors; works in three phases (connect, transfer, disconnect) and has flow control.
wrong: Saying confirmed connectionless has flow control or a connect phase.
Saying unconfirmed connectionless guarantees delivery.
Anything that contradicts the notes.
not_required: Layer or protocol examples.

required: The problem is unfairness: a station's advantage or disadvantage depends on its position on the bus.
It concerns reserving transmission rights: the position changes how well a station can reserve.
wrong: Saying all stations are treated equally, or that position does not matter.
Anything that contradicts the notes.
not_required: Which positions are favoured.
Details of how DQDB works beyond this.

required: Control plane: decides the routes (manages the network graph, defines routes, updates the switches' flow tables), or handles packets the data plane could not process; one of these is enough.
Data plane: forwards packets; the switches only execute the actions in their flow tables, which the control plane decided.

Names two controller tasks from: configuring forwarding tables, injecting packets, handling events from switches (packet-in), collecting or monitoring traffic statistics, topology discovery, inventory of devices and their capabilities, interfacing with control applications (northbound), interacting with the data plane (southbound), implementing the control plane.
wrong: Swapping the planes (data plane deciding routes, control plane forwarding packets).
Anything that contradicts the notes.
not_required: Control plane being logically centralized but physically distributed.
Which two tasks are named, beyond being correct controller tasks.

required: At least four distinct correct differences between the UDP and TCP headers. Each counts once: header size (UDP 8 bytes, much shorter than TCP 20-60 bytes); fixed length in UDP versus variable in TCP; each field only TCP has (sequence number, acknowledgment number, reserved, flags, advertised window, urgent pointer, options and padding) stated as being in TCP and not UDP; UDP has a packet length field while TCP has header length / data offset; source port optional in UDP but needed in TCP to establish the connection.
wrong: A header size that contradicts 8 bytes for UDP and 20-60 bytes for TCP.
Saying TCP has a fixed length or UDP a variable one.
Saying UDP has sequence numbers, acknowledgment numbers, flags or a window field.
not_required: Which four differences, and listing every field.

required: No: the independence assumption does not hold for real internet traffic.
Why: real traffic comes in bursts, so the chance of an arrival is influenced by earlier arrivals; arrivals are not independent.
wrong: Saying the assumption holds, or that real traffic is Poisson.
Saying traffic is bursty but arrivals are still independent.
not_required: The video streaming example or any other example.

required: The table holds a mapping between destinations (stations, MAC addresses) and the outgoing LAN interface to reach them.
Backwards learning starts from an empty table; until a destination is known, frames are flooded on all lines.
When a frame arrives with source address Q on LAN L, the bridge adds the entry 'Q can be reached over L': it learns from the source addresses of the traffic it observes.
Entries carry a timestamp, used to update or purge old entries.
Forwarding: look up the destination and send the frame only on the matching link (selective forwarding) instead of flooding.
One benefit: less duplication or unnecessary flooding, less congestion, or better bandwidth use than flooding.
wrong: The table maps IP addresses, or is filled in from destination addresses.
Saying the table is configured by hand rather than learned from traffic.
Anything that contradicts the notes.
not_required: Promiscuous mode.
Which benefit is named, beyond being a correct one.

required: First challenge: named and described, from the lecture's list (adaptation to moving nodes and topology changes; security; medium access such as hidden, exposed, near and far terminals; QoS; scalability; heterogeneity; dependability; power consumption). The description must say what makes it harder than in a fixed wired network.
Second challenge: a different one, named and described in the same way.
wrong: A challenge whose description contradicts the notes (e.g. hidden terminals described as nodes that can hear each other).
Challenges that apply equally to fixed wired networks, with no mobile or wireless reason.
not_required: Which two are chosen, and the A, B, C, D example from the lecture figure.

required: First benefit, with its reason: one of reduced switch complexity (switches just follow flow tables, no local routing decisions); faster convergence to a global optimum thanks to centralized routing with a global view; better integration of applications and network; increased flexibility (update routing logic on the fly, an API to program the network, high-level languages). A bare label with no reason does not count.
Second benefit, a different one, with its reason.

First drawback, with its reason: one of high complexity of the control servers (they make all routing decisions, so can be a bottleneck); dependence on centralized control (availability; more control servers bring synchronization and consistency issues, the CAP problem); cost and effort of adopting the technology (switching, training staff); security concerns (loss of hardware security).
Second drawback, a different one, with its reason.
wrong: Describing SDN switches as making their own routing decisions, or SDN routing as decentralized.
A benefit or drawback that contradicts the notes.
not_required: The CAP term, ROI, or naming the category when the reasoning is clear.

required: What it is: a network management protocol for IP networks in which a DHCP server dynamically assigns an IP address and other network configuration parameters to each device.

What it is used for, at least one: simplifies installation and configuration of end systems; allows manual and automatic IP address assignment; can provide additional configuration (DNS server, netmask, default router).
wrong: Describing another protocol's job (e.g. looking up names or mapping addresses) instead of assigning addresses and configuration.
Saying the device assigns addresses to the server.
not_required: That DHCP replaced RARP and BOOTP.
The extra parameters beyond IP address.

required: The requirement: two-way communication between sender and receiver (a full-duplex or semi-duplex connection), or frames that have an extra field for the acknowledgement; either one is enough.
wrong: Saying one-way (simplex) communication is enough.
Anything that contradicts the notes.
not_required: Explaining how piggybacking saves frames.
